tagline: A buffalo trace turned Shaker road, from Lebanon to the Ohio.
intro: US 68 crosses the Bluegrass on the line of an old buffalo trace that became a Shaker road in the 1800s. The designated byway comes in three pieces, about 104 miles in all, from Lebanon by Perryville and Harrodsburg, from Lexington by Paris, and from the Licking River up to Maysville and the Ohio state line. Along the way go black and white plank fences, big horse barns, tobacco fields and limestone rock fences.

In 1830 Andrew Jackson vetoed federal money for a turnpike company meant to join Lexington to Washington and Maysville, seeing it as a road inside one state, and that state the home of his rival Henry Clay.

moments.title: Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill
moments.text: A visitor in 1857 reported that the Shakers had kept one hired man at work for twelve years building stone walls around their fields, and that he had finished forty miles of them.

moments.title: Blue Licks Battlefield
moments.text: At salt springs where buffalo herds once wore the ground bare, Kentucky militiamen rushed into a battle in August 1782 that killed 60 of them, Daniel Boone's son Israel among them.

moments.title: Washington
moments.text: In 1833 a Cincinnati teacher named Harriet Beecher, visiting a student here, watched a slave auction in front of the old courthouse, one of the things that led her to write Uncle Tom's Cabin.
